> 夫兵者，不祥之器，物或惡之，故有道者不處.

Chapter 30 controlled the hand: have the result, and stop there. Chapter 31 addresses what the hand cannot reach — the heart.

"Winning felt good" does not live in the hand. It lives in the mouth, in the face, in that one sweet moment. Chapter 30 forbade fighting again; chapter 31 forbids finding it good.

So this chapter is not about tactics. It does something else: it names a thing.

## 不祥之器 is a classification, not a sermon

夫兵者，不祥之器 — weapons are an inauspicious instrument.

This is not moralizing. 不祥 is a category from ritual practice: 祥 is auspicious, aligned with what brings increase; 不祥 is what belongs to the register of loss, mourning, and death.

The 器 that belongs to that register is not forbidden. It is classified. And classification determines how it may be carried: when it can be borrowed, and when it cannot be lived with.

Once you know a tool belongs to the mourning register, you know what to do with it: use it when required, put it down after, do not keep it in the room.

## 物或惡之，故有道者不處

Some things dislike it, and so the one who has the way does not dwell there.

Same 處 as chapter 24's 有道者不處. Not "does not use" — does not reside. An army is sometimes necessary; a garrison is a residence.

## 君子居則貴左，用兵則貴右

In ordinary life the left is honored; in war the right is honored.

The 左/右 distinction is ritual position: 左 is the place of yang, of life, of the auspicious; 右 is the place of yin, of death, of mourning.

So the line is not a custom. It is a statement that the same person, entering war, moves to the other side of the room. The relation to the act changes with the position one stands in.

## 恬淡為上

> 不得已而用之，恬淡為上.

When forced to use it, 恬淡 is best. 恬 is calm; 淡 is thin, without flavor — the taste turned down to its minimum.

恬淡 is not indifference. Indifference would be a form of enjoying it. It is the palate deliberately kept from registering the sweetness, because the sweetness is what turns a necessary act into a preferred one.

## 勝而不美

> 勝而不美，而美之者，是樂殺人.

Win, and do not find it beautiful. To find it beautiful is to enjoy killing.

The word is 美 — beautiful, admirable, aesthetically pleasing. Not "do not be glad"; 美 is stronger and stranger: it forbids the aesthetic conversion of the victory.

This is the chapter's real target. The danger is not brutality, which is visible and can be restrained. It is the aestheticization of brutality: the parade, the medal, the story in which the killing becomes glorious. Once that conversion happens, the constraint is gone, because the act now produces beauty.

## 喪禮處之

> 殺人之眾，以悲哀泣之，戰勝以喪禮處之.

For the numbers killed, weep with grief; for the victory, conduct it as a funeral.

The 偏將軍居左，上將軍居右 passage is a ritual detail: the lower officer stands in the honored left position, the commander in the mourning right — the arrangement is inverted because the occasion is a funeral, not a triumph.

This is the most concrete instruction in the chapter, and the least likely to be practiced: the victory ceremony is to be a burial.

## The two chapters together

Chapter 30: the result is enough.
Chapter 31: and do not taste it.

Together they define the only configuration in which force does not corrupt: use it because it is forced, stop at the result, and refuse the pleasure.

Which is not a doctrine of passivity. It is a doctrine about what happens to a person who learns to enjoy the exercise of power — the enjoyment is the mechanism by which 不得已 converts into 取強.
